subject: Stan with big data? parallel libraries?

messages.author: b71a113cd1f5d048
messages.subject: Stan with big data? parallel libraries?
parts:
Hi All,

I've seen a bit of discussion about the scalability of Stan (including a nice plot by Bob C., I think) with big data.  And, I've found a few threads about Stan and MPI / OpenMP (pun intended).  Still, I'm not clear on whether Stan can farm out computations across processors/cores, as might be done with a large number of conditionally independent, e.g., likelihood factors. To be clear, I'm not talking about the relatively popular Stan topic of parallel chains, but more along the lines of parallelizing computations within iterations.  I anticipate data sets on the order of 10^5 or 10^6 observations (tree rings, btw), and I wonder how Stan will handle such big data.  More specifically, can Stan leverage a large number of cores (not for parallel chains necessarily!)?

Best,

Jarrett

To be clear, I'm not talking about the relatively popular Stan topic of parallel chains, but more along the lines of parallelizing computations within iterations.  I anticipate data sets on the order of 10^5 or 10^6 observations (tree rings, btw), and I wonder how Stan will handle such big data.  More specifically, can Stan leverage a large number of cores (not for parallel chains necessarily!)?

Basically, no. Assuming you are working with a Linux server that has a relatively recent g++, you could manually edit the .cpp file to do some stuff with OpenMP along the lines of

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/439

which Bob seemed to say would be safe. But you could easily get worse performance if you unvectorize a vectorizeable sampling statement. And at the point you are editing C++ files, you might as well put the OpenMP stuff into the likelihood function(s) you are using under $STAN_HOME/src/stan/prob .

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with big data? parallel libraries?
parts:
10^6 isn't that much data, but it depends what you do with it.

We don't have any immediate plans to parallelize computations
within chains, though we are well aware of the potential benefits
and trends in computing. The real puzzle is how we could deal with
autodiff, which requires substantial synchronization.

One thing we might be able to do is parallelize matrix operations.
For most of them, we're just operating on double values and
computing analytic derivatives, which we piece back together.
That'd only help with big matrices.

The other alternative would be to break down functions into
blocks that have independent gradients, then we can compute the
block and get its partials, then put everything back together.
We haven't even begun to think about how to do that --- I don't
see how we could write a smart enough compiler to do it
automatically.

- Bob
